terms.gloss: soft; of the mind, sensitive, easily moved
terms.grammar: adjective, third declension; ad + gerundive for what one is sensitive to
evidence: Cic. Att. 1.17.2: quam mollis animus et ad accipiendam et ad dēpōnendam offēnsiōnem
terms.comment: Cicero’s word for his brother Quintus, quick to take offence and quick to drop it. Its first sense is soft to the touch (see soft); of character it can also be weak or effeminate, so the context must show the kindly sense.

evidence: Hor. Ep. 2.2.102: genus vātum, the touchy tribe of poets (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: tender, delicate (of skin, a young plant, a child)
terms.comment: Sensitive in body: tenera cutis, sensitive skin.

terms.grammar: adjective, third declension, one ending; with the genitive
evidence: Tac. Hist. 2.99: mīles impatiēns sōlis, pulveris, tempestātum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Post-Augustan (Lewis & Short): sensitive to the sun, to cold. For the cold, Varro and Pliny have alsiōsus (M-O s.v. cold-sensitive).

phrases.latin: nam quanta sit in Quīntō frātre meō cōmitās, quanta jūcunditās, quam mollis animus et ad accipiendam et ad dēpōnendam offēnsiōnem, nihil attinet mē ad tē, quī ea nōstī, scrībere
phrases.english: how kind my brother Quintus is, how pleasant, how sensitive, quick to take offence and quick to let it go, there is no need for me to tell you, who know it

phrases.latin: inrītābilīs animōs esse optimōrum saepe hominum et eōsdem plācābilīs
phrases.english: that the best people are often touchy, and just as easily calmed

sources: Lewis & Short: mollis · Lewis & Short: irritabilis · Lewis & Short: tener · Lewis & Short: impatiens
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. sensitive; cold-sensitive.
Cicero’s letters to Atticus checked against the Perseus Latin texts (11 November 2026).
